---
title: Merge Strategies
---
Three buttons sit on a GitHub pull request, and they do genuinely different
things to history. Picking one is a decision you make once per repository, so it
is worth understanding what each leaves behind.

## The one Git has that GitHub does not

A **fast-forward** creates nothing. `main` is just a pointer, and if every commit
on `main` is already an ancestor of the branch, merging means sliding that
pointer forward.

```{mermaid}
gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    branch feature
    checkout feature
    commit id: "C"
    commit id: "D"
    checkout main
    merge feature id: "pointer moves"
```

```shell
git checkout main && git merge --ff-only feature
```

`C` and `D` keep their exact SHAs, author dates, committer dates and signatures.
`main` and `feature` end up pointing at the identical commit. If `main` has moved
on at all, git refuses rather than inventing anything — that refusal is the
feature.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **GitHub has no fast-forward button.** Not in the merge UI, not in `gh pr
> merge`. A true fast-forward can only be done locally and pushed. Every GitHub
> merge strategy creates new commits.

## The three GitHub offers

### Merge commit

Keeps every commit and adds one more that joins the two lines.

```{mermaid}
gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    branch feature
    checkout feature
    commit id: "C"
    commit id: "D"
    checkout main
    commit id: "B"
    merge feature id: "merge commit"
```

History is a truthful record of what happened in parallel, and it is a thicket
to read. `git log --graph` becomes necessary rather than optional. Common on
older repositories and on release-branch models.

### Squash and merge

Collapses the whole branch into one new commit on `main`.

```{mermaid}
gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    commit id: "squashed PR"
```

One commit per pull request. The branch's individual commits are discarded —
they survive only on the closed PR page. **This is the most common default at
companies**, because it makes `main` a clean list of shipped changes and it
means nobody has to care how messy a branch was mid-review.

The consequence worth internalising: the **PR title and body become the commit
message**. Writing a good PR description is not politeness, it is the permanent
record.

### Rebase and merge

Replays each commit from the branch onto the tip of `main`, one at a time.

```{mermaid}
gitGraph
    commit id: "A"
    commit id: "B"
    commit id: "C'"
    commit id: "D'"
```

Linear like a fast-forward, and every commit survives individually. But `C'` and
`D'` are **copies**: same content, new SHAs, new committer dates. The originals
are left orphaned on your local branch.

## Side by side

| | `--ff-only` (local only) | Merge commit | Squash | Rebase |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| New commits created | none | one | one | one per commit |
| Original SHAs | preserved | preserved | discarded | **rewritten** |
| Author date | preserved | preserved | new | preserved |
| Committer date | preserved | preserved | new | **rewritten to merge time** |
| GPG signatures | preserved | preserved | lost | broken or re-signed |
| History shape | linear | branching | linear | linear |
| Individual commits kept | yes | yes | **no** | yes |
| Works when `main` moved on | **no** | yes | yes | yes |

That last row is the whole reason GitHub omits fast-forward. On a shared
repository `main` almost always has commits your branch does not, so the one
operation that never works is a poor button.

## What a rewrite does to your local branch

After a rebase or squash merge, your local branch and `main` hold **identical
content under different commits**. Git reports this as divergence:

```shell
$ git diff dev origin/main          # empty — content is the same
$ git rev-list --count origin/main..dev   # 41
$ git rev-list --count dev..origin/main   # 41
```

Forty-one commits "ahead" and forty-one "behind" with no actual difference. Each
of your commits has a twin on `main` that git cannot recognise as the same
thing.

> [!WARNING]
> **Never `git merge` to fix this.** Merging replays all your originals on top of
> their own copies and duplicates the entire branch.

**Allowed**

```shell
git checkout dev && git reset --hard origin/main
```

**Not allowed**

```shell
git checkout dev && git merge origin/main     # duplicates every commit
```

The cleaner habit avoids the problem entirely: **let the branch die at the
merge.** Branch per change, delete it after, branch again from a fresh `main`.
Divergence cannot happen to a branch that no longer exists.

```shell
git checkout main && git pull
git checkout -b fix/some-thing
# work, commit, push, open PR, merge in the browser
git checkout main && git pull
git branch -d fix/some-thing
```

Set **Automatically delete head branches** in repository settings and GitHub
deletes the remote side for you.

## Anything derived from a commit date

A rewrite moves the **committer** date and leaves the **author** date alone.

| Format | Meaning | Survives a rebase |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `%aI` | when the change was written | **yes** |
| `%cI` | when the commit object was last created | no |

Any script reading `git log -1 --format=%cI` will see every commit in a merged
PR change timestamp at merge time. Use `%aI` unless you specifically want to
know when it landed.

## What I do here

Repository settings restrict this to **rebase only** — merge commits and squash
are switched off, so the wrong button cannot be clicked by accident.

Rebase over squash because commits here are written to stand alone, and squash
would flatten a deliberately separated set into one. Rebase over a local
fast-forward because merging in the browser is what collaboration looks like,
and the practice is worth more than exact SHAs on a personal repository.

The accepted costs: SHAs are rewritten, the local branch needs `reset --hard`
after each merge, and anything reading `%cI` churns once per merge.

## Enforcing the choice

Repository settings, so the decision is structural rather than remembered:

- `Settings → General → Pull Requests` — uncheck **Allow merge commits** and
  **Allow squash merging**, check **Automatically delete head branches**.
- `Settings → Rules → Rulesets` on `main` — **Require a pull request before
  merging** and **Require linear history**. This is what stops a habitual push
  straight to `main`.

```shell
gh api -X PATCH repos/OWNER/REPO \
  -F allow_merge_commit=false -F allow_squash_merge=false \
  -F allow_rebase_merge=true  -F delete_branch_on_merge=true
```
